handbook-ironworking-text:
Ironworking Expanded is the iron tier: everything you need to smelt iron in bulk before you own a single boiler. It is deliberately self-sufficient - the whole chain runs off an axle and a waterwheel, and nothing in it needs steam.

The loop. Crushed iron ore, crushed coke and lime flux go into an Ore Mixer, which blends them into burden - the prepared charge. Burden is stockpiled in an Ore Bunker and dropped into the Cold Blast Furnace, which is blown with cold air from a Twin-Tub Blower and renders the charge down to molten pig iron and slag. The pig runs out of a tap into a molten canal, which plumbs it to wherever you want to cast it.

Pig iron is not a finished metal. It is hard, brittle and useless for tools - it is the shared intermediate everything downstream is made from. Remelt it in a Cupola Furnace with scrap and you get cast iron, which casts into machine parts and substitutes for vanilla iron in build recipes. Work it down instead and you get wrought iron, which is vanilla iron. Steel comes later, and needs the steam tier.

What the iron tier leaves behind. Bolted pipe - the first of three pipe tiers - and the molten-canal network, both of which every later tier builds on. Cast iron tools and parts. And slag, which is not waste: it lays as paths, slabs and stairs.

Where to start. Build the ore mixer first - nothing else works without burden. Then the furnace, then a blower on an axle. The canal can wait: pig solidifies at the tap and can be chiselled out by hand until you have somewhere better to send it.
handbook-orehandling-text:
The furnace does not eat ore. It eats burden - a blended charge of crushed iron ore, crushed coke and lime flux. Burden cannot be crafted by hand; it comes out of an Ore Mixer, and preparing it well is most of what decides how your furnace runs.

The Ore Mixer is a megablock driven by an axle. Load it with the three components and it blends them into burden, stamping the mix it made onto the output: how much iron, how much flux, how much fuel. That stamp travels with the item, survives being split and stacked, and is what the furnace reads when you charge it. Block-info names the grade it produced and flags a charge that is off-spec or short of flux.

Coke is the number that matters. A coke-rich burden burns hot and blows easily, but eats fuel and drinks air. A coke-lean burden saves fuel - and packs so dense that the blast can barely get through it, so it demands far more pressure than a hand-driven blower can raise. At the iron tier you run rich burden and accept the fuel cost; running lean is what the steam tier is for.

Blocks required:
- 1 x Ore Mixer (axle-driven)
- 1 x Ore Bunker (any burned-brick colour)
- 1 x Tall Hopper, over the furnace shaft

The Ore Bunker is the buffer between them: burden in, burden out, one heat's worth at a time. Its front opening accepts a vanilla chute or Archimedes screw, so a mixer, a bunker and a hopper can be strung together to charge the furnace on their own while you do something else.

Coke, not coal. Coke is baked from coal in a coke oven; raw coal in the mixer makes a charge the furnace will grade as off-spec. Crush the ore and the coke in a pulverizer. Even scrap iron bits crush back into crushed iron and go round again.

One pile, one melt. The mixer packs burden dense - a single full pile holds most of a heat, so you are not shuttling stacks all day.
handbook-coldblastfurnace-text:
The Cold Blast Furnace is the iron tier's primary smelter: a tall open-topped stack of refractory brick that reduces ore burden to molten pig iron. It smelts ore and only ore - it will not take scrap. For that you want the cupola.

Building it. Place the Cold Blast Furnace Core first - it is the bottom-centre anchor the whole build hangs off - then ctrl + shift + rightmouse it to see the build outline, and fill in every highlighted block until it reports complete.

Blocks required:
- Refractory Bricks (any tier; the core takes on the tier you build it from)
- 1 x Cold Blast Furnace Core (the anchor, placed first)
- 2 x Tuyere, low on the shaft
- 2 x Molten Metal Tap - the lower for iron, the upper for slag
- 1 x Tall Hopper, over the shaft
The shaft inside is left hollow. That is where the burden goes.

There is no door. The open top of the stack is its chimney - the furnace vents straight up and recycles nothing, which is exactly what makes it the cold blast furnace. A finished furnace is cleared by breaking its walls. Do not stand on the charge: a player who falls into a working furnace does not come out.

Blowing it. The two tuyeres are pipe nodes - run bolted pipe from a Twin-Tub Blower to them and the blower will fill the line. How much pressure the furnace needs depends on the charge: a coke-rich burden blows through easily, a lean one packs dense and needs more than a mechanical blower can raise. If the line will not hold pressure, check that the run is sealed - an open pipe end vents to atmosphere.

Firing it. Let the hopper fill the shaft, ignite the burden, and the furnace climbs on its own. It has no fixed maximum temperature: what it reaches is a balance between the heat the coke and the blast put in, and what the stack radiates away and the cold charge soaks up. A rich burden on cold blast settles comfortably past iron's 1482 C melting line. A lean one stalls short of it, and no amount of patience will help - it needs preheated blast, which needs the steam tier.

Block-info always shows the current temperature, the threshold it is trying to clear, and both sides of the ledger, so a stall reads as a number and not as a mystery.

Tapping it. Once it is Melting, molten pig collects behind the lower tap and slag behind the upper. Open a tap and the metal runs out. With nothing plumbed to it, it solidifies at the tap and is chiselled free by hand; with a molten canal under it, it runs off to be cast properly.

The fire is fragile. Running out of burden, choking the tuyeres, or letting the blast die all count against the furnace, and enough of it puts the fire out.
handbook-moltencanals-text:
Molten metal is plumbed, not carried. You never pick liquid iron up. It leaves a furnace tap into a molten canal and flows, cell by cell, to wherever you built the canal to go.

Every cell owns its own metal. A canal is not a pipe with one shared pool - each block holds what is standing in it, and each tick some of it moves to the next cell along. That is why a long canal takes visible time to deliver, and why a canal left standing full slowly goes solid: metal cools where it sits. A solidified cell is not lost, but you will be chiselling it out.

The pieces:
- Canal Start - sits under a furnace tap and takes the runout
- Canal (straight, bend, T-junction, cross) - the run itself
- Canal Tap - drains the run out; park a barrel under it to fill
- Mold Pedestal - pours into a mold set on it, which is how you cast
- Molten Barrel - a standalone vessel for holding a heat

Building a run. Every canal shape can be cut from cobblestone, from coloured running brick, or from fire brick - hammered and chiselled over fire clay. The rock or brick you use is cosmetic; pick whichever you have. A T-junction forks a heat between two stations, which is how one tap feeds a mold and a barrel at once.

Taps are shut by default. A closed tap severs the run at that point, so metal backs up behind it instead of draining. Open it with rightmouse when you actually want the run to empty.

Casting. Set a mold on a Mold Pedestal and the pedestal pours into it from the canal it is fed by. Cast iron parts, ingots and tool blanks all come out this way. What you can cast depends on what is in the canal - pig from the blast furnace, cast iron from the cupola.

Slope is not modelled. Metal moves along connectors, not downhill, so a canal can run level. What it cannot do is cross a gap: every cell must touch the next.
handbook-designtable-title: Ironworking: Diagrams and the Design Table
handbook-designtable-text:
The Design Table is where plans are drawn. A diagram is a reusable crafting plan: it goes in the grid alongside the raw material, tells the recipe which shape to make, and - because it is a tool, not an ingredient - it is not consumed. Draw a plan once and build from it forever.

Why bother. Without diagrams, every shape of every part needs its own grid pattern, and a pipe network's four shapes across three material tiers is twelve patterns to memorise. With them there is one pattern per part - plan plus material - and the plan picks the shape. The same straight-canal diagram cuts a straight canal out of any rock you feed it.

Blocks required:
- 1 x Design Table

Using a diagram. Put it in the crafting grid with the material the recipe calls for - for a molten canal, cobblestone. The output takes the shape the diagram names and the material you supplied, and the diagram comes back out unharmed.

This is a young system. The molten canal shapes are the first parts to use it, and more will move over. Existing hand-patterned recipes keep working alongside it, so nothing you have already learned stops working.
